ai-apps.whyMoney: Recurring software revenue with AI attach pricing on top; the layer where model capability converts into seats, usage and workflow lock-in.
ai-apps.whyFail: Foundation models commoditize thin wrappers; incumbents bundle AI for free; token costs eat gross margin if pricing is per-seat while costs are per-use.
ai-apps.bottleneck: Distribution and proprietary data/workflow context — not model access, which everyone has.
ai-apps.metrics:
AI product ARR / attach rate
Net revenue retention
Gross margin trend vs inference cost
Seat growth vs usage growth
ai-apps.redFlags:
AI features given away without pricing
GM compression from token costs
Churn to platform-native AI

model-labs.whyMoney: Frontier capability rents: whoever owns the best model taxes every downstream app; consumer subscriptions and enterprise API usage scale with capability.
model-labs.whyFail: Training costs compound faster than revenue; open-weights models cap pricing; capability converges and the moat collapses to distribution.
model-labs.bottleneck: Compute access and unique data; talent concentration in a handful of teams.
model-labs.metrics:
API + subscription revenue run-rate
Compute commitments vs funding
Capability benchmark gaps vs open weights
Enterprise seat expansion
model-labs.redFlags:
Open-weights parity on frontier tasks
Training run economics deteriorating
Key research team departures

hyperscalers.whyMoney: They rent the buildout back to everyone: AI capex becomes contracted cloud revenue with multi-year visibility, and in-house silicon fattens margins over time.
hyperscalers.whyFail: Depreciation wave from GPU fleets outruns AI revenue; a capex pause exposes overbuild; regulators cap the OpenAI/Anthropic equity-compute loops.
hyperscalers.bottleneck: Power and land for new regions; GPU allocation; the ROI debate between capex and free cash flow.
hyperscalers.metrics:
Cloud AI revenue growth vs total capex
RPO / backlog growth
Capex-to-revenue ratio trend
In-house silicon mix
hyperscalers.redFlags:
Any hyperscaler guiding capex down
AI revenue disclosures going vague
Depreciation schedule shortening

neoclouds.whyFail: Leveraged GPU depreciation bets: if utilization or renewal pricing slips, debt service eats the equity; hyperscalers can undercut at will.
neoclouds.bottleneck: Powered shells and GPU allocation today; refinancing terms tomorrow. Contract quality (tenor, counterparty, take-or-pay) is everything.
neoclouds.metrics:
Contracted backlog and tenor
Customer concentration
Cost of debt / lease structure
Utilization and renewal pricing
Power secured (MW) vs deployed
neoclouds.redFlags:
Anchor-tenant renegotiation
Financing spreads widening
Merchant (uncontracted) capacity growing
GPU resale values falling

custom-silicon.whyMoney: Design-win annuities: every hyperscaler wants its own accelerator, and the ASIC partner collects NRE plus per-unit royalties without merchant inventory risk.
custom-silicon.whyFail: Programs are lumpy and cancellable; customers eventually in-source; the merchant GPU stays good enough and the ASIC never ramps.
custom-silicon.bottleneck: SerDes/interconnect IP and advanced-node design talent; packaging slots at TSMC.
custom-silicon.metrics:
Named program count and ramp timing
ASIC revenue growth vs GPU market
Content per accelerator
Next-gen program renewals
custom-silicon.redFlags:
A flagship program cancelled or in-sourced
Competing ASIC vendor winning sockets
NRE-heavy mix without unit follow-through

semi-ip.whyMoney: Royalty per chip with near-zero marginal cost: chiplets and AI SoC complexity multiply the licensable blocks per design; revenue lags design wins then compounds.
semi-ip.whyFail: Royalty rates get squeezed by big customers; RISC-V and in-house IP erode the base; small players stay sub-scale forever.
semi-ip.bottleneck: Standard ownership (interconnect, die-to-die) and switching costs baked in at architecture time.
semi-ip.metrics:
ACV growth
Royalty revenue vs license mix
Design wins reaching production
Royalty per chip trend
semi-ip.redFlags:
Royalty renegotiations downward
RISC-V displacement wins
ACV stall with rising opex

eda.whyMoney: A duopoly toll booth on every chip design ever taped out; AI design complexity raises tool intensity and AI-assisted flows add a new pricing layer.
eda.whyFail: China export bans remove a large market; design-start recessions; open-source or AI-native challengers eventually attack the flow.
eda.bottleneck: Engineer trust and flow lock-in; hardware emulation capacity for AI-scale verification.
eda.metrics:
Backlog growth
Hardware/emulation demand
China revenue exposure
AI flow attach pricing
eda.redFlags:
Bookings deceleration
China restrictions broadening
Customer consolidation squeezing pricing

foundries.whyMoney: Physical scarcity: only one or two fabs on earth can print leading-edge AI silicon, and pricing power compounds each node while customers have no alternative.
foundries.whyFail: Geopolitical tail risk on Taiwan; a capex arms race into a demand air pocket; a rival finally executing at 2nm.
foundries.bottleneck: EUV tool allocation, advanced packaging capacity, and fab construction timelines (3-4 years).
foundries.metrics:
Leading-edge utilization and pricing
AI revenue share and growth
CoWoS/packaging capacity ramp
Overseas fab yield parity
foundries.redFlags:
Cross-strait escalation
N2 yield or schedule slip
Customer dual-sourcing at scale

packaging.whyMoney: The current binding constraint on GPU supply: CoWoS-class capacity is sold out years forward, and every HBM stack and chiplet design adds packaging content.
packaging.whyFail: Capacity catches up and scarcity pricing evaporates; the technology shifts (panel-level, glass) and strands existing tools.
packaging.bottleneck: Interposer capacity, HBM stacking yield, and precision bonding equipment lead times.
packaging.metrics:
CoWoS-equivalent capacity vs bookings
Packaging content per accelerator
Yield on advanced stacks
New entrant capacity announcements
packaging.redFlags:
Packaging capacity glut forming
Technology transition stranding tools
GPU vendor insourcing packaging

memory.whyMoney: AI turned bandwidth into the scarce input: HBM is sold out on long-term agreements at premium margins, and a three-player oligopoly is finally behaving rationally.
memory.whyFail: Memory is still a commodity cycle — an overbuild or AI demand pause brings back brutal ASP declines; NAND stays structurally oversupplied.
memory.bottleneck: HBM stacking capacity and yield; TSV throughput; qualification slots at NVDA/AMD.
memory.metrics:
HBM sold-out horizon and pricing
DRAM/NAND spot vs contract
Inventory weeks at customers
Capex discipline across the big three
memory.redFlags:
HBM qualification loss
Inventory build at hyperscalers
Capex race resuming
NAND dumping spreading to DRAM

optical.whyMoney: Copper runs out of reach as speeds hit 224G+: every rack-to-rack link goes optical, transceiver content per GPU keeps climbing, and 1.6T is the next leg.
optical.whyFail: Brutal China-based price competition; co-packaged optics resets the value chain; hyperscalers qualify cheaper second sources fast.
optical.bottleneck: Indium-phosphide capacity, laser yield, and hyperscaler qualification cycles.
optical.metrics:
800G/1.6T shipment mix
Gross margin trend
Design wins per hyperscaler
CPO adoption timeline
optical.redFlags:
ASP erosion accelerating
CPO leapfrogging pluggables
Share loss to Chinese vendors

cxl.whyMoney: If memory pooling standardizes, the fabric layer earns IP and silicon content on every disaggregated server — early, optionality-rich, licensing-led.
cxl.whyFail: CXL adoption keeps slipping; NVLink-style proprietary fabrics win instead; the market stays niche for a decade.
cxl.bottleneck: Ecosystem readiness — CPUs, OS support, and hyperscaler willingness to re-architect memory.
cxl.metrics:
CXL attach on new server platforms
Pooling deployments at scale
Fabric silicon design wins
cxl.redFlags:
Standard fragmentation
Hyperscalers passing on pooling
Proprietary fabric lock-in expanding

servers.whyMoney: Someone has to bolt the racks together: AI server ASPs are 10-20x traditional, and integration complexity (liquid cooling, NVLink domains) adds real value-add margin.
servers.whyFail: It is still contract manufacturing — margins are thin, customers are concentrated, and hyperscalers can shift orders overnight.
servers.bottleneck: GPU allocation, liquid-cooling integration capability, and rack-scale validation capacity.
servers.metrics:
AI server revenue and backlog
Gross margin per rack trend
Customer concentration
Liquid-cooled mix
servers.redFlags:
Margin compression on flagship programs
Order shifts between ODMs
Inventory build of GPU systems

dc-realestate.whyMoney: Powered land is the new scarcity: whoever controls energized shells near fiber can sign decade-long leases at rising rates with investment-grade tenants.
dc-realestate.whyFail: Rates gap out against long-duration leases; hyperscalers self-build; a capex pause leaves speculative shells empty.
dc-realestate.bottleneck: Grid interconnection queues (3-5 years) and utility power allocations — not land or capital.
dc-realestate.metrics:
Leasing volume and pre-lease rates
Re-leasing spreads
Power banked (MW) vs contracted
Development yield vs cost of capital
dc-realestate.redFlags:
Speculative vacancy rising
Re-leasing spreads compressing
Tenant credit deterioration

grid.whyMoney: Transformers, switchgear and HV equipment have multi-year lead times and no spare capacity — data-center demand meets a grid already needing replacement.
grid.whyFail: Capacity additions eventually catch up; utility procurement cycles slow; a demand pause strands expanded factories.
grid.bottleneck: Transformer manufacturing capacity and grain-oriented electrical steel; skilled electrical labor.
grid.metrics:
Backlog and book-to-bill
Lead time trends
Price realization
Utility capex budgets
grid.redFlags:
Lead times normalizing fast
Order cancellations
Capacity expansions outrunning demand

ups.whyMoney: Every AI megawatt needs backup and conditioning; UPS and battery content scales with density, and lithium systems refresh the installed base.
ups.whyFail: Component commoditization; Chinese battery-backed entrants; hyperscalers redesigning around centralized DC power architectures.
ups.bottleneck: Power-electronics supply and installation labor more than technology.
ups.metrics:
DC segment order growth
Backlog conversion
Content per MW trend
ups.redFlags:
Architecture shifts cutting UPS content
Price competition from Asia
Order push-outs

cooling.whyMoney: Rack power density is making air cooling physically impossible — liquid transition re-prices the entire thermal stack, with content per rack up 5-10x.
cooling.whyFail: Liquid cooling commoditizes fast (it is plumbing at scale); GPU vendors standardize reference designs that squeeze differentiation.
cooling.bottleneck: Cold-plate and CDU manufacturing capacity; facility retrofit engineering talent.
cooling.metrics:
Liquid-cooling orders and mix
Content per rack trend
Reference-design wins
Service attach
cooling.redFlags:
Commoditization pressure on CDUs
OEM in-sourcing thermal
Order lumpiness masking share loss

construction.whyMoney: The buildout is ultimately a construction project: whoever can deliver substations, shells and fit-outs on schedule owns a decade of backlog at improving margins.
construction.whyFail: Skilled-labor inflation eats fixed-price contracts; a capex pause empties the pipeline; execution stumbles on mega-projects.
construction.bottleneck: Electricians and craft labor — the least elastic input in the entire stack.
construction.metrics:
Backlog / RPO growth
Margin on new bookings
Labor availability and wage trends
Project mix shift toward DC/power
construction.redFlags:
Fixed-price mega-project overruns
Backlog growth stalling
Labor cost spiral

materials.whyMoney: Copper, rare earths and specialty inputs are the long tail nobody can substitute: grid plus DC demand meets decade-long mine development timelines.
materials.whyFail: Commodity beta dominates — a macro downturn swamps the AI demand signal entirely; substitution and thrifting at high prices.
materials.bottleneck: Permitting and mine development timelines (7-10 years); refining concentrated in China.
materials.metrics:
Copper deficit projections vs price
DC/grid share of demand growth
Inventory levels
Supply disruptions
materials.redFlags:
Demand destruction at high prices
China growth rolling over
New supply arriving early

semi-equip.whyMoney: Every new fab and node transition buys the same oligopoly tools: litho, etch, deposition and metrology margins compound through cycles, with services annuities on top.
semi-equip.whyFail: WFE is cyclical and China pull-forward reverses; export controls chop a third of the market; a node delay pauses everything.
semi-equip.bottleneck: EUV availability, subsystem supply chains, and China policy.
semi-equip.metrics:
WFE guidance revisions
Leading-edge vs memory mix
China revenue share
Services growth
Backlog cover
semi-equip.redFlags:
China revenue cliff
Memory capex freeze extending
Leading-edge push-outs

ai-data.whyMoney: Models are hungry and the web is exhausted: labeling, curation, and synthetic data pipelines get paid per token of training fuel, with RLHF expertise scarce.
ai-data.whyFail: Synthetic data and self-play cut the human-labeling market; labs in-source; it is a services business wearing a software multiple.
ai-data.bottleneck: Expert-labeler supply for frontier domains (code, math, science) — commodity labeling is already commoditized.
ai-data.metrics:
Revenue per customer and concentration
Gross margin (services vs platform)
Frontier-lab relationships
Synthetic data mix
ai-data.redFlags:
Anchor customer in-sourcing
Pricing per task collapsing
Lab consolidation shrinking buyers

observability.whyMoney: Every AI workload ships with monitoring, security and cost-management attach: usage-based models ride inference growth without touching model risk.
observability.whyFail: AI-native challengers rebundle the stack; usage optimization cycles; hyperscalers give away good-enough tooling.
observability.bottleneck: Enterprise trust and data gravity — switching an observability stack is a multi-year project.
observability.metrics:
Net revenue retention
AI-cohort revenue disclosure
Platform module attach
Usage vs committed contracts
observability.redFlags:
NRR erosion
AI features cannibalizing paid SKUs
Seat-based pricing breaking down

databases.whyMoney: AI apps need governed, queryable data with vector search bolted in: the platforms holding enterprise data tax every RAG pipeline built on top.
databases.whyFail: Postgres eats everything from below; hyperscaler-native services bundle; consumption models cut both ways in downturns.
databases.bottleneck: Data gravity and governance requirements — the data is already in someone's platform.
databases.metrics:
Consumption growth and NRR
AI workload attach
Competitive win rates vs Databricks/Postgres
Margin trajectory
databases.redFlags:
Consumption optimization waves
Open-source parity
AI workloads landing elsewhere

edge.whyMoney: Inference moves on-device for latency, privacy and cost: NPU content raises silicon value per phone, PC, car and camera — licensing and chip vendors both win.
edge.whyFail: Killer on-device AI apps keep not arriving; cloud inference gets too cheap; content gains get competed away in mature markets.
edge.bottleneck: Power-efficient NPU design and the software toolchains that make heterogeneous compute usable.
edge.metrics:
NPU content per device trend
AI-PC / AI-phone mix
Auto design-win pipeline
Royalty per unit
edge.redFlags:
AI features failing to drive upgrades
Content pricing competed away
Auto programs slipping

robotics.whyMoney: Embodied AI is the next compute sink: if foundation models crack manipulation, robots become the largest silicon and sensor market ever created.
robotics.whyFail: The demo-to-deployment gap stays wide for another decade; unit economics never close against human labor; capital dries up.
robotics.bottleneck: Training data for the physical world; reliability at 99.99%; cost-down of actuators and sensors.
robotics.metrics:
Deployed units generating revenue
Cost per robot trend
Task reliability benchmarks
Backlog from real customers
robotics.redFlags:
Pilot purgatory (demos, no deployments)
Cash burn without unit economics
Humanoid hype outrunning capability

financing.whyMoney: Someone must fund a multi-trillion-dollar buildout: private credit and infra funds collect fees and spreads on data-center debt, GPUs and power deals.
financing.whyFail: They are the leverage in the system — if AI cash flows disappoint, the credit losses land here first; spread compression as everyone piles in.
financing.bottleneck: Deal quality: underwriting GPU collateral and merchant power is genuinely new territory.
financing.metrics:
Fee-related earnings growth
Infra/credit fundraising
DC-related deployment volume
Realized spreads and default rates
financing.redFlags:
GPU-collateralized loan losses
Spread compression
Fundraising slowdown
Mark-downs on infra books

items.makes: GPU cloud at hyperscale — the largest independent NVIDIA fleet, contracted to Microsoft/OpenAI.
items.moat: Scale, NVIDIA relationship (allocation + investment), and multi-year take-or-pay backlog.
items.different: The only neocloud operating at genuine hyperscale with anchor contracts to match.
items.bull: Backlog converts and diversifies; refinancing keeps working; becomes the fourth cloud.
items.bear: Leverage + customer concentration + GPU depreciation is a fragile tripod.

items.makes: Full-stack AI cloud (ex-Yandex) plus data services and edge bets.
items.moat: Real engineering culture and owned software stack, not just racks; strong cash position from the Yandex unwind.
items.different: Builds like a tech company, not a datacenter REIT — software differentiation.
items.bull: Microsoft-scale deals repeat; capacity milestones land; software margin on top of compute.
items.bear: Sub-scale vs giants; must keep raising to keep building.

items.makes: Owned renewable-powered sites converting from BTC mining to AI cloud.
items.moat: Cheap owned power and land bank with grid connections already secured.
items.different: Power-first: owns the electrons rather than renting them.
items.bull: Conversion economics beat building new; AI contracts fill capacity at software-like ROIC.
items.bear: Two-business identity crisis; GPU financing risk on a miner balance sheet.

items.makes: Purpose-built AI campuses (Ellendale) leased to neoclouds/hyperscalers.
items.moat: Speed to energized capacity in a power-short market; Macquarie capital partnership.
items.different: The landlord model — builds and leases shells rather than operating GPUs.
items.bull: Ellendale leases up fully financed; repeatable campus playbook.
items.bear: Highest leverage in the group; single-project, single-tenant concentration.

items.makes: Post-bankruptcy HPC hosting; large CoreWeave colocation contracts.
items.moat: Existing energized sites — scarce, immediately monetizable capacity.
items.different: Restructured balance sheet renting to the neocloud rather than competing with it.
items.bull: Contract expansions and strategic interest keep re-rating the asset base.
items.bear: One tenant is most of the story; power costs and renewal terms can turn.

items.makes: Lithography — EUV and High-NA; the only maker of leading-edge litho on earth.
items.moat: A literal monopoly with a 20-year technology lead and an irreplaceable supplier network (Zeiss).
items.different: No competitor exists; every leading-edge roadmap routes through it.
items.bull: High-NA extends the monopoly a decade; 2026-27 order inflection on N2/18A.
items.bear: Order lumpiness, China DUV cliff, and customer capex discipline.

items.makes: Broadest portfolio: deposition, etch, implant, CMP, metrology, packaging.
items.moat: Breadth + scale — sells into every fab regardless of which node or memory type wins.
items.different: The diversified index of WFE; least single-technology risk.
items.bull: GAA + backside power + packaging inflections all expand its served market.
items.bear: China exposure and memory cyclicality still swing the P&L.

items.makes: Etch and deposition; dominant in high-aspect-ratio NAND and HBM TSV etch.
items.moat: Process-of-record lock-in at memory makers; services annuity on the installed base.
items.different: The most memory-levered of the majors — highest torque to a memory recovery.
items.bull: NAND recovery plus HBM capacity buildout double-hits its sweet spot.
items.bear: Memory capex discipline caps the upcycle; China restrictions bite.

items.makes: Process control — inspection and metrology; the yield police of every fab.
items.moat: Near-monopoly in optical inspection; highest margins in WFE; data moat from every wafer inspected.
items.different: Sells certainty, not throughput — spend rises as nodes get harder regardless of unit growth.
items.bull: Inspection intensity rises every node; packaging metrology is a new leg.
items.bear: Largest China mix among majors; leading-edge delays hit hardest.

items.makes: Inspection and metrology for advanced packaging — HBM stacks and chiplets.
items.moat: Focused leadership in a niche the majors under-served until it exploded.
items.different: A pure small-cap play on packaging inspection, not front-end WFE.
items.bull: HBM4 and chiplet complexity multiply inspection steps per device.
items.bear: KLA/Onto push into the niche; lumpy orders from few customers.
